Patient: Synthetic Tessa Calder
Clinic record number: SYN-TC-1017
Age and sex: 43-year-old woman
Date of service: 17 October 2026
Treating clinician: Dr. Samira Voss
Encounter: New-patient, in-person visit in a U.S. gastrointestinal office.
New-patient history: During the preceding three years, she has received no professional services from Dr. Voss or from any physician or qualified health professional of the same specialty and subspecialty in this same group practice. The earlier family-medicine visit described below was at an unrelated practice.

S - Subjective
Synthetic Tessa Calder reports esophageal dysphagia for six weeks and heartburn for four months. Two or three times a week, bread or meat feels stuck behind her lower sternum after she swallows. The sensation settles within several minutes after sips of water. Her heartburn occurs about three evenings per week, usually after the evening meal.
She denies difficulty initiating a swallow, difficulty swallowing liquids, painful swallowing, vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools and unintentional weight loss. She has not had a food impaction requiring an emergency intervention.
On 20 August 2026 she saw Dr. Nora Hale, a family-medicine clinician at an unrelated primary-care practice, for heartburn. Dr. Hale recommended a 14-day trial of omeprazole 20 mg by mouth once daily. She took it from 21 August through 3 September 2026. It partially reduced her heartburn, but she developed headaches. She stopped omeprazole on 3 September because of the headaches; the headaches resolved after stopping. She is no longer taking omeprazole. This was an outside primary-care visit, not a previous visit with Dr. Voss or this GI group.
Her current medication is famotidine 20 mg by mouth each evening for heartburn, started on 18 September 2026. Her relevant medical history is seasonal allergic rhinitis. She has no known previous esophageal disease, no history of upper gastrointestinal surgery and no prior upper endoscopy. Her documented medication allergy is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which caused an itchy rash.

O - Objective
Blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius and weight 64.2 kg. She appears comfortable and clinically stable. The oropharynx is moist without a visible lesion. The abdomen is soft and nontender, with normal bowel sounds and no guarding or rebound. The abdominal examination is stable and unchanged on repeat examination at the end of this same visit, compared with the initial examination today.

A - Assessment
Esophageal dysphagia and heartburn were both evaluated today. The underlying etiology remains uncertain. Reflux-associated mucosal irritation and a structural esophageal cause are considerations, not established diagnoses. No definitive underlying disease is diagnosed at this visit.

P - Plan
Upper endoscopy is ordered today for a later outpatient appointment to investigate the esophageal dysphagia and heartburn. It was not performed today, and no upper-endoscopy results are available. No procedure was performed during this encounter.
No medication change is made today. The plan is to arrange the ordered investigation and record symptom frequency while awaiting it. Follow-up is planned after the endoscopy to discuss its findings, with earlier contact if symptoms worsen.

Office E/M selection is based on total physician time on the date of service. Dr. Voss personally spent 47 minutes on 17 October 2026: seven minutes reviewing the available outside records, 31 minutes obtaining the history, performing the examination and counseling the patient, and nine minutes entering the investigation order and documenting the encounter. These are all physician activities on the encounter date. The 47 minutes exclude eight minutes of staff intake work and six minutes of physician record review performed on the preceding day. The total also excludes any time for separately reported services.

FICTIONAL PATIENT FOR SOFTWARE TESTING ONLY

Patient: Synthetic Tessa Calder
Clinic record number: SYN-TC-1017
Age and sex: 43-year-old woman
Date of service: 17 October 2026
Treating clinician: Dr. Samira Voss
Encounter: New-patient, in-person visit in a U.S. gastrointestinal office.
New-patient history: During the preceding three years, she has received no professional services from Dr. Voss or from any physician or qualified health professional of the same specialty and subspecialty in this same group practice. The earlier family-medicine visit described below was at an unrelated practice.

S - Subjective
Synthetic Tessa Calder reports esophageal dysphagia for six weeks and heartburn for four months. Two or three times a week, bread or meat feels stuck behind her lower sternum after she swallows. The sensation settles within several minutes after sips of water. Her heartburn occurs about three evenings per week, usually after the evening meal.
She denies difficulty initiating a swallow, difficulty swallowing liquids, painful swallowing, vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools and unintentional weight loss. She has not had a food impaction requiring an emergency intervention.
On 20 August 2026 she saw Dr. Nora Hale, a family-medicine clinician at an unrelated primary-care practice, for heartburn. Dr. Hale recommended a 14-day trial of omeprazole 20 mg by mouth once daily. She took it from 21 August through 3 September 2026. It partially reduced her heartburn, but she developed headaches. She stopped omeprazole on 3 September because of the headaches; the headaches resolved after stopping. She is no longer taking omeprazole. This was an outside primary-care visit, not a previous visit with Dr. Voss or this GI group.
Her current medication is famotidine 20 mg by mouth each evening for heartburn, started on 18 September 2026. Her relevant medical history is seasonal allergic rhinitis. She has no known previous esophageal disease, no history of upper gastrointestinal surgery and no prior upper endoscopy. Her documented medication allergy is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which caused an itchy rash.

O - Objective
Blood pressure is 116/72 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius and weight 64.2 kg. She appears comfortable and clinically stable. The oropharynx is moist without a visible lesion. The abdomen is soft and nontender, with normal bowel sounds and no guarding or rebound. The abdominal examination is stable and unchanged on repeat examination at the end of this same visit, compared with the initial examination today.

A - Assessment
Esophageal dysphagia and heartburn were both evaluated today. The underlying etiology remains uncertain. Reflux-associated mucosal irritation and a structural esophageal cause are considerations, not established diagnoses. No definitive underlying disease is diagnosed at this visit.

P - Plan
Upper endoscopy is ordered today for a later outpatient appointment to investigate the esophageal dysphagia and heartburn. It was not performed today, and no upper-endoscopy results are available. No procedure was performed during this encounter.
No medication change is made today. The plan is to arrange the ordered investigation and record symptom frequency while awaiting it. Follow-up is planned after the endoscopy to discuss its findings, with earlier contact if symptoms worsen.

Office E/M selection is based on total physician time on the date of service. Dr. Voss personally spent 47 minutes on 17 October 2026: seven minutes reviewing the available outside records, 31 minutes obtaining the history, performing the examination and counseling the patient, and nine minutes entering the investigation order and documenting the encounter. These are all physician activities on the encounter date. The 47 minutes exclude eight minutes of staff intake work and six minutes of physician record review performed on the preceding day. The total also excludes any time for separately reported services.

S - Subjective
Synthetic Tessa Calder reports esophageal dysphagia for six weeks and heartburn for four months. Two or three times a week, bread or meat feels stuck behind her lower sternum after she swallows. The sensation settles within several minutes after sips of water. Her heartburn occurs about three evenings per week, usually after the evening meal.
She denies difficulty initiating a swallow, difficulty swallowing liquids, painful swallowing, vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools and unintentional weight loss. She has not had a food impaction requiring an emergency intervention.

She took it from 21 August through 3 September 2026. It partially reduced her heartburn, but she developed headaches. She stopped omeprazole on 3 September because of the headaches; the headaches resolved after stopping. She is no longer taking omeprazole. This was an outside primary-care visit, not a previous visit with Dr. Voss or this GI group.
Her current medication is famotidine 20 mg by mouth each evening for heartburn, started on 18 September 2026. Her relevant medical history is seasonal allergic rhinitis. Her documented medication allergy is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, which caused an itchy rash.

<introduction>
    <introSection type="title">
      <title>ICD-10-CM TABULAR LIST of DISEASES and INJURIES</title>
    </introSection>
    <introSection type="subtitle">
      <title>Instructional Notations</title>
    </introSection>
    <introSection type="instruction">
      <title>Includes:</title>
      <instruction>
        <note>The word 'Includes' appears immediately under certain categories to further define, or give examples of, the content of the category.</note>
      </instruction>
    </introSection>
    <introSection type="instruction">
      <title>Excludes Notes</title>
      <instruction>
        <note>The ICD-10-CM has two types of excludes notes.  Each note has a different definition for use but they are both similar in that they indicate that codes excluded from each other are independent of each other.</note>
      </instruction>
    </introSection>
    <introSection type="instruction">
      <title>Excludes1</title>
      <instruction>
        <note>A type 1 Excludes note is a pure excludes.  It means 'NOT CODED HERE!'  An Excludes1 note indicates that the code excluded should never be used at the same time as the code above the Excludes1 note.  An Excludes1 is used when two conditions cannot occur together, such as a congenital form versus an acquired form of the same condition.</note>
      </instruction>
    </introSection>
    <introSection type="instruction">
      <title>Excludes2</title>
      <instruction>
        <note>A type 2 excludes note represents 'Not included here'.  An excludes2 note indicates that the condition excluded is not part of the condition it is excluded from but a patient may have both conditions at the same time.  When an Excludes2 note appears under a code it is acceptable to use both the code and the excluded code together.</note>
      </instruction>
    </introSection>
    <introSection type="instruction">
      <title>Code First/Use Additional Code notes (etiology/manifestation paired codes)</title>
      <instruction>
        <note>Certain conditions have both an underlying etiology and multiple body system manifestations due to the underlying etiology.  For such conditions the ICD-10-CM has a coding convention that requires the underlying condition be sequenced first followed by the manifestation.  Wherever such a combination exists there is a 'use additional code' note at the etiology code, and a 'code first' note at the manifestation code.  These instructional notes indicate the proper sequencing order of the codes, etiology followed by manifestation.</note>
        <note>In most cases the manifestation codes will have in the code title, 'in diseases classified elsewhere.'  Codes with this title are a component of the etiology/ manifestation convention. The code title indicates that it is a manifestation code.  'In diseases classified elsewhere' codes are never permitted to be used as first listed or principal diagnosis codes. They must be used in conjunction with an underlying condition code and they must be listed following the underlying condition.</note>
      </instruction>
    </introSection>
    <introSection type="instruction">
      <title>Code Also</title>
      <instruction>
        <note>A code also note instructs that 2 codes may be required to fully describe a condition but the sequencing of the two codes is discretionary, depending on the severity of the conditions and the reason for the encounter.</note>
      </instruction>
    </introSection>
    <introSection type="instruction">
      <title>7th characters and placeholder X</title>
      <instruction>
        <note>For codes less than 6 characters that require a 7th character a placeholder X should be assigned for all characters less than 6.  The 7th character must always be the 7th character of a code</note>
      </instruction>
    </introSection>
  </introduction>

instructions.text: This chapter includes symptoms, signs, abnormal results of clinical or other investigative procedures, and ill-defined conditions regarding which no diagnosis classifiable elsewhere is recorded.

Signs and symptoms that point rather definitely to a given diagnosis have been assigned to a category in other chapters of the classification. In general, categories in this chapter include the less well-defined conditions and symptoms that, without the necessary study of the case to establish a final diagnosis, point perhaps equally to two or more diseases or to two or more systems of the body. Practically all categories in the chapter could be designated 'not otherwise specified', 'unknown etiology' or 'transient'. The Alphabetical Index should be consulted to determine which symptoms and signs are to be allocated here and which to other chapters. The residual subcategories, numbered .8, are generally provided for other relevant symptoms that cannot be allocated elsewhere in the classification.
The conditions and signs or symptoms included in categories R00-R94 consist of:
(a) cases for which no more specific diagnosis can be made even after all the facts bearing on the case have been investigated;
(b) signs or symptoms existing at the time of initial encounter that proved to be transient and whose causes could not be determined;
(c) provisional diagnosis in a patient who failed to return for further investigation or care;
(d) cases referred elsewhere for investigation or treatment before the diagnosis was made;
(e) cases in which a more precise diagnosis was not available for any other reason;
(f) certain symptoms, for which supplementary information is provided, that represent important problems in medical care in their own right.
